texts.preamble: S.Rahim vs The State Of Kerala on 9 March, 2016 Author: B.Sudheendra Kumar Bench: B.Sudheendra Kumar In The High Court Of Kerala At Ernakulam Present: The Honourable Mr. Justice B.Sudheendra Kumar Wednesday, The 9Th Day Of March 2016/19Th Phalguna, 1937 Crl.Rev.Pet.No. 1923 of 2010 ( ) --------------------------------- Crl.A 806/2008 of Sessions Court, Thiruvananthapuram Cc 90/2001 of J.M.F.C.-Ii, Thiruvananthapuram Revision Petitioner(S)/Appellant/Accused: ---------------------------------------- S.Rahim, S.N.Stores, T.C.39/205(1), Kothuval Street, Chalai, Thiruvananthapuram. By Advs.Sri.Ram Mohan.G. Sri.G.P.Shinod Respondent(S)/Respondents/State And Complainant: ------------------------------------------------ 1. The State Of Kerala, Represented By The Public Prosecutor, High Court Of Kerala, Ernakulam. 2. C.L.Dileep, Food Inspector, Corporation Of Thiruvananthapuram, Thiruvananthapuram. R By Public Prosecutor Sri.R.Githesh This Criminal Revision Petition Having Been Finally Heard On 09-03-2016, The Court On The Same Day Passed The Following: S.Rahim vs The State Of Kerala on 9 March, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/10233727/ 1 Scl. texts.facts: 2. Heard. 3. The prosecution allegation can be briefly stated thus:- On 7.12.2000 at about 2.30 p.m., PW1, the Food Inspector purchased 750 gram of black gram from the revision petitioner. After sampling as per rules, one sample was sent to the Public Analyst for analysis. The public analyst after analysis submitted Ext.P11 report stating that the sample contained talc an inorganic pigment and was therefore adulterated under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955. Thereafter, on the request of the revision petitioner, the second sample was sent to the Central Food Laboratory for analysis. Ext .P18 certificate of the Central Food Laboratory would also show that the sample did not conform to the standard prescribed for urd whole under the PFA Rules, 1954 as the sample showed the presence of talc content and was therefore adulterated. In this case, the sample was said to be misbranded and adulterated on the basis of Exts.P11 and P18 report of analysis. 4. Before the trial Court, PW1 to PW4 were examined and Exts.P1 to P18 were marked for the prosecution. DW1 and DW2 were examined and Ext.D1 was marked for the revision petitioner.
texts.arguments: 5. The learned counsel for the revision petitioner has submitted that since no laboratory for the analysis of the food item was defined and no validated method of analysis was prescribed as per the mandate of Section 23 (1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the PFA Act, Ext.P18 cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased by the Food Inspector was misbranded or adulterated. The learned counsel for the revision petitioner relied on the decision of the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176] to buttress his argument. It was held by the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) that since the Laboratories were not notified and the tests conducted by such laboratories were not admissible in evidence, no prosecution could be based on such report and the accused was entitled to get acquittal. In the decision of this Court in Gopalakrishnan v. Food Inspector [2013 (3) KLT 455], the court relied on the decision of the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) and found that the Public Analyst's report was not admissible in evidence and accordingly, the Court acquitted the accused.
